Kṛti.--From one passage in the Rigveda, where the Maruts are described as having Kṛtis, Zimmer concludes that the word means a dagger used in war. But there is no evidence that kṛti was ever a human weapon. See asi.
Foot notes i. 168, 3.
Altindisches Leben, 301. Cf. Schrader, Prehistoric Antiquities, 221.

1. Kṛttikās are unquestionably Tauri, etc., the Pleiades. The names of the seven stars forming this constellation, and given above from yajurveda texts, include three--abhrayantī, ‘forming clouds’; meghayantī, ‘making cloudy’; varṣayantī, ‘causing rain’--which clearly refer to the rainy Pleiades. The word kṛttikā possibly means ‘web,’ from the root kṛt, ‘spin.’
Foot notes taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 4, 5, 1; kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xl. 4; Taittīrīya brāhmaṇa, iii. 1, 4, 1.

Kṛtvan.--In one passage of the Rigveda the word kṛtvan in the plural is mentioned with the Ārjīkas and the five peoples. Pischel thinks that it means a people, and Sāyaṇa expressly says that the Kṛtvans designate a country. The name in that case would point to some connexion with the Kurus or Krivis. Hillebrandt, however, thinks that the word is an adjective which qualifies Ārjīkas and designates this people as magicians, being applied to them by an opponent. In favour of this view, he quotes Hiouen Thsang's statement that the neighbouring kings held the base Kaśmīrians in such scorn as to refuse all alliance with them, and to give them the name of Ki-li-to, or Kṛtyas. He suggests that the Ārjīkas settled in Kasmīr in ancient times already had the same evil reputation as their successors in later days.
Foot notes ix. 65, 23.
Vedische Studien, 2, 209.
